l5hu-focus: Heads-Up: The Ultimate Test of Decision Density

HU is the highest-decision-density poker format: you're in a blind every hand, 200+ hands/hour, and nearly every hand sees a flop. This means your focus in HU is both a weapon and a weakness — one lapse can miss the opponent's tendencies, miscalculate odds, or lose emotional control during high-frequency downswings. HU pros treat focus as a trainable resource, not innate talent.

HU focus isn't "staring at the screen" but "maintaining the same quality across high-frequency decisions". Use session-length limits + state awareness + fatigue control so the last hand's decision quality matches the first.

HU state-management three principles: (1) session-length limit — HU focus is hard to sustain beyond 60-90 minutes; preset the time and stop on schedule, avoiding fatigue-induced decision deterioration; (2) variance budget — pause and review after losing 40-50BB, a stop-and-restart not a chase; (3) stand up every 100 hands — break losing-streak inertia and rest your eyes and mind. Fatigue signs include: starting to play marginal hands, losing bet-sizing control, repeating low-level mistakes, and ignoring the opponent's obvious tendencies.

Example: You've played HU for 2 hours straight; in the last 30 hands you've been "auto-playing" — not noticing the BB's fold rate vs your C-Bets dropped from 45% to 30%. That's a classic fatigue sign: your awareness of opponent deviations dulled and you still bet at the old frequency, getting harvested by the opponent's counter-adjustment. Correct move: pause immediately, recognize fatigue, rest, and restart with "how is the opponent playing now" rather than "how do I usually play".

Example 2 (state-management flow): Set three rules before the HU session: (1) maximum 90 minutes; (2) stop at 50BB down; (3) stand up 2 minutes every 100 hands. Execute strictly on schedule even when the table is hot — because "winners also give the edge back when tired". Tendler emphasizes: discipline isn't limiting fun but protecting long-term EV.

Counterintuitive point: the most dangerous thing in HU isn't "impulse when losing" but "letting your guard down after winning". After winning a few hands, players often relax, play marginal hands, and give the edge back. HU discipline must be consistent throughout, win or lose.

Theory support: the variance density and emotional triggers of heads-up play are covered in Theory Academy T8 "Pressure Management" — that chapter splits sustained tension into variance density, time pressure and self-talk, and gives an actionable cooling-down move for each; the triad in this lesson is the three that fit cash heads-up best.

Theory support: the types of emotional breakdown and the decision drift they cause are covered in Theory Academy T8 "Tilt Typology" — first name which breakdown is yours (revenge, ego, or the easy-to-miss fatigue type), then talk countermeasures; swap "I tilted today" for "which type did I tilt as" and discipline finally has a handle.
HU session-management triad: (1) preset a variance budget — pause and review after losing 40-50BB; (2) stand up every 100 hands to break losing-streak inertia; (3) review only EV, never results.

Focus in three lines:
About 200 hands per hour, so a 90-minute cap equals roughly 300 decisions — the quality of the last few dozen decides the real EV of the session
Fatigue shows up first as dulled awareness (for example the fold rate against your C-Bets falls from 45% to 30% and you never notice), not as "one bad hand"
A 40-50BB variance budget plus standing up every 100 hands (about 30 minutes) writes stop-loss into the process instead of leaving it to willpower
l5hu-opponent-psychology: Heads-Up: The Battlefield of Reading People

HU faces one opponent, so reading people is amplified enormously — you don't juggle multiple table images, just this one player. Opponent psychology (Reading) splits into two types: behavior patterns (bet sizes, calling tendencies, tilt tendencies) and real-time signals (bet rhythm, reaction time). In HU the two combine to help you infer the opponent's range and emotional state.

Reading isn't guessing hands — it's estimating ranges + emotions. "Calls too fast" may mean a marginal or strong hand; "thinks too long" may mean a tough decision or acting. Convert observations into probabilities, not certainties.
Reading Bet Rhythm and Reaction Time

Bet rhythm and reaction time are important signals in HU (especially online). Common readings: betting too fast = possibly a strong hand (eager for value) or a weak hand (not wanting to overthink); thinking too long = a tough decision (marginal hand/draw) or acting; hesitant calls = marginal hands. But these signals are unreliable with insufficient samples — cross-verify with 50-100 hand frequency statistics; a single rhythm doesn't count.

Example: The HU opponent thinks 20 seconds before calling your turn bet. Frequency read: long think = a tough decision, possibly a marginal hand (station trait) or a draw. But with insufficient samples it could be acting. Correct approach is cross-verification: his tendency to call big bets, his river showdown choices — judge comprehensively rather than relying on one rhythm alone.

Example 2 (counter-reading): You hold AA and watch your rhythm when betting the flop. If you bet instantly because "I have a strong hand" and hesitate because "I'm bluffing", the opponent will quickly crack you. Counter-reading drill: set the same think time for all bets, or deliberately break rhythm at key moments (hesitate with strong, be decisive with bluffs). You read the opponent, and the opponent reads you.

Counterintuitive point: the enemy of reads isn't "reading wrong" but "overconfidence". HU pros admit "this read is only 60% sure" and bet accordingly, rather than "I know what he has". Converting reads into probabilities rather than certainties is the sustainable strategy.

Theory support: the full street-by-street narrowing flow with blocker filtering is covered in Theory Academy T7 "Heads-Up Hand Reading" — draw a starting range from the preflop action, narrow it street by street in a Bayesian way, then use blockers to delete impossible strong combos; this lesson compresses all of that into "reading means estimating a range".

Theory support: observation and counter-observation are covered in Theory Academy T8 "Psychological Reads" — that chapter puts "I read him" and "he reads me" on the same table, explaining why a one-sided read gets cancelled by the opponent counter-read, and why a consistent rhythm is the cheapest counter-reading solution.

Read discipline: (1) only conclude from statistically significant frequencies (50+ hand samples); (2) cross-verify bet rhythm with frequency; (3) admit read uncertainty and fold it into equity and pot-odds calculations. After these three, reads go from mysticism to math.

Reading in three lines:
Reading means estimating range plus emotion, writing observations as probabilities ("about 45% bluff") rather than verdicts ("he is bluffing")
A single timing tell is unreliable: at about 200 hands per hour, a 50-hand sample takes only about 15 minutes — gather the sample before concluding
Counter-reading costs the immediate edge that rhythm provides and buys long-term unreadability; both sides of the ledger have to be counted

l5hu-focus-q1.question: The core of HU focus is:
options: Staring at the screen without distraction
Maintaining the same quality across high-frequency decisions, via session limits and fatigue control
l5hu-focus-q1.explanation: HU focus is "maintaining quality across high-frequency decisions", achieved through state management like session-length limits, variance budgets, and periodic breaks.

l5hu-focus-q2.question: The reasonable upper limit of an HU session length is about:
l5hu-focus-q2.explanation: HU focus is hard to sustain beyond 60-90 minutes; overtime causes decision deterioration. Fatigue risk is extremely high beyond 3 hours.

l5hu-focus-q3.question: Which is NOT a typical fatigue sign?
options: Being more aware of opponent tendencies
l5hu-focus-q3.explanation: Fatigue dulls awareness of opponent tendencies rather than sharpening it. Marginal hands, sizing control loss, and low-level mistakes are fatigue signs.

l5hu-focus-q4.question: The role of the "pause at 50BB" variance budget is:
options: Limiting the maximum you can lose
Pausing for review at the stop-loss point, avoiding chase-style re-buying
l5hu-focus-q4.explanation: A variance budget is stop-loss discipline: pause and review at the preset point, cutting the "get even" impulse and avoiding fatigue and tilt.

l5hu-focus-q5.question: The correct statement about HU discipline is:
options: You can extend time when the table is hot
Discipline must be consistent throughout, win or lose
Discipline is only needed when losing
l5hu-focus-q5.explanation: Relaxation after winning and fatigue are equally dangerous. HU discipline must be consistent throughout — no relaxation in either direction — to protect long-term EV.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q1.question: The correct way to read people in HU is:
options: Estimating ranges + emotions, converting observations into probabilities
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q1.explanation: Reading is estimating ranges + emotions, converting observations into probabilities rather than certainties. Single-hand impressions are unreliable.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q2.question: The common reading of "betting too fast" in HU is:
options: Possibly strong (eager for value) or weak (not wanting to overthink) — cross-verify
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q2.explanation: Betting too fast may be strong (eager for value) or weak (not wanting to overthink); a single signal is unreliable and needs cross-verification with frequency statistics.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q3.question: The online HU opponent thinks 20 seconds before calling your turn bet. The most reliable handling is:
options: Judge him marginal and raise immediately
Cross-verify with his tendency to call big bets and his showdown choices
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q3.explanation: A long think may mean marginal/draw/acting; a single instance is unreliable. Cross-verify with frequency like his big-bet call tendency and river showdown choices.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q4.question: The core of "counter-reading (Balanced Play)" is:
options: Making actions not leak range information, keeping rhythm consistent or breaking it
Making the opponent unable to guess hand strength
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q4.explanation: Counter-reading requires actions not to leak range: no "fast with strong, slow with weak" — keep rhythm consistent or deliberately break it.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q5.question: The correct attitude toward HU reads is:
options: Admitting uncertainty and folding it into equity and pot-odds calculations
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q5.explanation: Reads carry uncertainty; pros convert them into probabilities (like "60% sure") and fold them into decisions — the sustainable strategy.

l5hu-focus-q6.question: Heads-up runs about 200 hands per hour and the session cap is 90 minutes. At that density, roughly how many hand decisions do you make in 90 minutes?
l5hu-focus-q6.explanation: 200 hands/hour × 1.5 hours = 300 hands. 200 treats 90 minutes as one hour; 600 comes from treating the cap as 3 hours, double the 60-90 minute window.

l5hu-focus-q7.question: At about 200 hands per hour, "stand up every 100 hands" means a break roughly every:
l5hu-focus-q7.explanation: 100 hands ÷ 200 hands/hour = 0.5 hours = 30 minutes. 60 minutes misreads the density as 100 hands/hour; 100 minutes reads hands as minutes.

l5hu-focus-q8.question: Fatigue keeps you betting at the old frequency while the opponent fold rate has already fallen from 45% to 30%. Pot 4BB, you bet 1.33BB (1/3 pot). Using EV = f × P − (1 − f) × b, the change in this street's EV is about:
l5hu-focus-q8.explanation: Old frequency EV = 0.45 × 4 − 0.55 × 1.33 ≈ +1.07BB; at 30% it becomes 0.30 × 4 − 0.70 × 1.33 ≈ +0.27BB; the difference is ≈ −0.80BB. −0.27 is the new overall EV and −1.07 the old overall EV — neither is the delta.

l5hu-focus-q9.question: Which of these is fatigue-driven decision degradation rather than a strategy choice?
options: Betting 1/3 pot on a dry high-card board
Not noticing the opponent fold rate fell from 45% to 30% and betting at the old frequency
Giving up a thin value bet on the river
Keeping only strong hands in the 3-bet value range
l5hu-focus-q9.explanation: The other three can all be sound strategy choices: you knew the information and decided accordingly. Only dulled awareness plus the old frequency is a state problem — the information changed and you did not update.

l5hu-focus-q10.question: You are down 45BB at a 100BB buy-in heads-up table, right inside the 40-50BB variance budget. The disciplined response is:
options: Top up to 100BB and raise bet sizes to win the 45BB back
Pause the session for review and end or reschedule per the preset rule
Raise the variance budget to 100BB and keep playing
Switch to another table and keep playing to avoid the same opponent
l5hu-focus-q10.explanation: A variance budget is stop-loss discipline: entering the 40-50BB band means pausing to review and cutting the get-even impulse. Topping up, raising the budget or moving tables all demote the budget from a rule to a suggestion.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q6.question: Heads-up runs about 200 hands per hour. Under the rule of concluding only from samples of 50+ hands, gathering 50 hands takes about:
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q6.explanation: 50 hands ÷ 200 hands/hour = 0.25 hours = 15 minutes. 50 minutes reads hands as minutes; 2 hours would already be about 400 hands, far past the bar.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q7.question: Pot 4BB, you bet 1.33BB (1/3 pot), and your read says the opponent folds about 50%. Using EV = f × P − (1 − f) × b, the expectation of this street is about:
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q7.explanation: EV = 0.5 × 4 − 0.5 × 1.33 = 2 − 0.665 ≈ +1.34BB. +2.00 counts only the fold side; +0.67 subtracts the whole 1.33 and forgets to weight it by the call probability.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q8.question: The cost of counter-reading (using the same think time for every bet) is:
options: Giving up part of the immediate rhythm edge in exchange for long-term unreadability
Making it easier for the opponent to judge your hand strength
Having to give up all bluffs
Having to think longer than the opponent
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q8.explanation: A consistent rhythm sacrifices immediate gains such as fast with strong and slow with weak, and buys the inability of the opponent to infer your range from timing. It neither bans bluffing nor changes the absolute think time.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q9.question: Pot 10BB, the opponent bets 5BB. Using the required-equity-to-call formula, the equity you need is:
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q9.explanation: Calling 5BB into a 20BB total pot (10 + 5 + 5) needs 5 ÷ 20 = 25%. 33.3% is 5 ÷ 15 and forgets your own 5BB; 20% miscounts the total pot as 25BB.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-q10.question: The opponent 3-bet 3 times in 12 hands (25%). Under reading discipline, the correct handling is:
options: Declare him a high-frequency 3-bettor and tighten the whole opening range
Treat it as a hypothesis, keep playing the baseline, and adjust after 50-100 hands
l5hu-opponent-psychology-q10.explanation: A 25% read over 12 hands has a very wide confidence interval and is not yet a frequency; treat it as a hypothesis, play the baseline, and keep logging to 50-100 hands. Tightening or counter-bluffing at once treats a hypothesis as a conclusion.

l5hu-focus-ex1.title: Fatigue-Induced Decision Deterioration
reasoning: JTs is a standard HU button open
In a normal state you should open actively
If tired and unaware of the BB's tendency change, pause rather than continue
l5hu-focus-ex1.mistakeAction: Auto-Fold or play marginal hands while fatigued
l5hu-focus-ex1.mistakeReasoning: Fatigue causes decision deterioration — not noticing the BB's fold-rate change or losing sizing control. The correct move is pausing to rest, not continuing.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-ex1.title: Reading With Rhythm and Frequency Combined
reasoning: KQ on a K-8-3 dry board is top pair
The BB's fold rate vs C-Bets is 50% (across 60 hands of stats)
After cross-verifying with the BB's calling tendencies, 1/3-pot thin value
l5hu-opponent-psychology-ex1.mistakeAction: Judging the BB weak based on one slow think
l5hu-opponent-psychology-ex1.mistakeReasoning: A single rhythm signal is unreliable; cross-verify with the 60-hand fold-rate statistics rather than relying on one reaction time alone.

l5hu-focus-ex2.title: Size Drift Under Fatigue
reasoning: AA is an overpair on K-9-4 rainbow: a 1/3-pot bet takes thin value and keeps the betting frequency high — the size does not need to grow because the hand is strong
Break-even fold rate at 1/3 pot = 1.33 ÷ (4 + 1.33) ≈ 25%: the opponent only has to fold the weakest quarter for the bet to profit
The classic fatigue error is scaling up to a 2x-pot overbet: 8BB needs 8 ÷ (4 + 8) ≈ 66.7% folds to break even, and a tired player is not even watching the fold rate
l5hu-focus-ex2.mistakeReasoning: An 8BB overbet needs about 66.7% folds just to break even. Sizing up usually comes from wanting to end the hand quickly rather than from what the board wants — the textbook form of sizing drift.

l5hu-focus-ex3.title: The Fatigued Hero Call
reasoning: The river is an 8BB bet into a 4BB pot: required equity to call = 8 ÷ (4 + 8 + 8) = 40%
AJ beats only pure bluffs: every Kx, two pair and straight beats it, and the value share of a 2x-pot bet is far above 60%
At minute 120 with fatigue signals already showing, wanting the chips back disguises itself as reading a bluff — that call is driven by emotion, not odds
l5hu-focus-ex3.mistakeReasoning: The 40% line requires at least 40% of a 2x-pot river bet to be bluffs, which such a size rarely supports in heads-up. Fatigue does not change the number; it only makes a losing call look like a read.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-ex2.title: River Bluff-Catch: Frequency Read Beats One Timing Tell
reasoning: Pot 18BB and a 9BB river bet: required equity to call = 9 ÷ (18 + 9 + 9) = 25%
Across 120 hands with showdowns checked, about 45% of his river bets at this half-pot size were bluffs — 45% clears the 25% bar
EV(call) = 0.45 × 27 − 0.55 × 9 = +7.2BB; if the read is off and the bluff share is 20%, it flips to 0.20 × 27 − 0.80 × 9 = −1.8BB, so this call lives on frequencies, not feelings
l5hu-opponent-psychology-ex2.mistakeAction: Fold (his timing was decisive, so it must be value)
l5hu-opponent-psychology-ex2.mistakeReasoning: A single timing tell is a weak signal: decisive can be value or a bluff decided long ago. Letting it override 120 hands of frequency data trades verifiable evidence for one impression.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-ex3.title: A Frequency Read Drives the Turn Check-Raise
reasoning: Across 80 hands, about 55% of his range folds to a check-raise at this size, and he has used a half-pot size on both streets — a wide betting tier that can be pressured
A check-raise to 12BB needs f ≥ 12 ÷ (12 + 12) = 50% to break even, and the read of 55% already clears it
15 outs (9 flush + 8 straight − 2 overlapping 8♣/K♣) give about 15 ÷ 46 ≈ 33% on one street, so being called still leaves a way out
l5hu-opponent-psychology-ex3.mistakeReasoning: Calling 4BB throws away the 55% fold rate: every fold would have handed over a 12BB pot, and a 15-out draw can afford the risk of being called.

l5hu-opponent-psychology-p3.tableDesc: Heads-up cash game; the SB's bet rhythm is abnormal

option.action: Min-raise 2BB and end the session at the preset time
option.explanation: T9s is a standard open on its own; the grading point here is state: 110 minutes is past the 60-90 minute cap, and mechanical sizing is a fatigue sign. Play the hand and end the session on schedule — that is discipline written into the process.

option.action: All-in 100BB to finish quickly while the feel is still there
option.explanation: A 100BB shove gets called only by strong hands and turns T9s into a pure bluff; finishing quickly is a product of fatigue, not board evidence.

option.action: Fold and save the chips for when you feel sharp again
option.explanation: Folding throws away a standard open with positive EV, and waiting until you feel sharp is the favourite excuse of fatigue. End the session instead of sitting there waiting to wake up.

l5hu-focus-p4.tableDesc: Heads-up cash game; 110 minutes in, the same sizing for the last 20 hands

option.action: Call 5BB and treat the last showdown as an unverified hypothesis
option.explanation: Required equity = 5 ÷ (13 + 5) ≈ 27.8%, and AQ top pair top kicker is far above that line. One showdown can only raise a hypothesis (he may check-raise bluff a lot); it takes 50-100 hands to make it a conclusion, so play the baseline until then.

option.action: All-in 94BB because he just check-raise bluffed with 7-5
option.explanation: Extrapolating one observation into a frequency is the most common overconfidence in reading. A shove gets called only by value and folds out the bluffs — the whole stack bet on a single piece of evidence.

option.action: Fold, top pair top kicker is always behind a check-raise
option.explanation: On a dry Q-7-2 board AQ top pair top kicker is nowhere near a fold; folding to a check-raise donates every bluff to the opponent.
